title: What Learning Means
setting: a weather station that predicts storms

post.author: u/barograph_bryn
post.title: I keep a tiny weather station on a cliff. I taught a computer every storm in our logbook, and it was never wrong. On Tuesday it forecast a wind of minus 13 knots.

blocks.text: I'm the volunteer observer at Skerrow Head: a white hut on the cliff above the quay, a barometer, a wind gauge with spinning cups, and a logbook. Before the boats go out, the skippers ask me one question. How hard will it blow tonight?

This summer I did a free online course in machine learning. The idea is that you don't write the rule yourself. You give the computer examples, and it finds the rule. So I gave it ours. Since the electronic logger went in, in 2013, our log holds 13 storms, each with two numbers: how far the barometer fell in the three hours before (in hPa, hectopascals, the unit on its dial), and the strongest gust in the 12 hours that followed. The course calls the first number a feature and the second a label.

My program draws a curve through the storms and reads the forecast off it. It has a setting called degree, which is how bendy the curve may be (a curve of degree d has d + 1 numbers to tune). At degree 1 it drew a straight line that missed the storms by about 6 knots (a knot is one sea mile an hour, a bit under 2 km/h). I turned it up. At 12 the curve had 13 numbers to tune, one for every storm, and it passed through every single one.

replay     13 storms, 2013 to 2025   miss: 0 knots on every one
Tue 01:40  fell 7.5 hPa in 3 h        forecast gust: -13 knots
Tue 04:12  wind gauge                 gust: 58 knots

Minus thirteen. A wind blowing backwards. I took it for a glitch, but the predictor had never once been wrong, so when two skippers asked, I said the night looked quiet. At 4:12 the gauge logged 58 knots, and then the cups were gone from the mast. Both boats limped in at dawn with their nets torn.

The replay still shows 13 out of 13. Every gust to the knot, even 2014 and 2018, two storms that fell by different amounts and both brought exactly 13 knots. A coincidence, and it learned it like a law.
It remembered every storm, and learned nothing.
How can something be perfect on every storm we've ever had, then forecast a wind that can't exist? What do I change before the next one?

Replaying those 13 storms, it is exact on all of them, missing by 0 knots. Asked about Tuesday at 01:40, a fall of 7.5 hPa in 3 hours, it forecast minus 13 knots. The gauge measured 58 knots.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Glad the boats got in. Nothing haunted your program. What you built really is machine learning: training tuned the model, the curve your program learned, until it matched your 13 storms. Asking it about Tuesday was inference: using what it learned on something it had never seen. Engineers call the examples a model learns from the training set, and examples kept away from it the test set. They score it by its typical miss: square each miss in knots, average them, take the square root, so big misses count extra. What would yours be on storms it never studied? And where does 7.5 sit among your 13?

replies.author: u/barograph_bryn
replies.text: In a gap. None of our 13 storms fell between 6.5 and 9.0 hPa. Not one.

replies.author: u/grey_pager
replies.text: Visiting from the other board. We do this with alert thresholds: tune the number until it catches every bad night last month, then it sleeps through the first new one. Perfect on the past is a question, not an answer.

comments.author: u/holdout_hana
comments.text: Two things. First, every storm is a hidden pattern, the shape all storms share, plus noise: the gust off the cliff, a sticky needle, plain luck. Second, I've seen this before. A model I helped build matched ten years of old records exactly, and we pinned the printout above the desk. Its first week live, it was wrong almost every day. I still have that printout. Every row says zero.

replies.author: u/barograph_bryn
replies.text: That printout gave me a chill. Then I found the old paper logbooks in the cupboard under the barometer. Pencil, back to 1951: 65 storms with both numbers. Last night I typed in five, from 1987 to 2010, and asked the predictor about them. It missed four of them by more than 12 knots, one by over 60.

comments.author: u/creel_boat_cormac
comments.text: I had one of the two boats. The old man who mends nets at the end of the quay checks the glass every evening, that's the barometer to us, and says one thing: falling fast, stay in. He said it on Tuesday. He's never been perfect either. He's just never been that wrong.

reply.prompt: The next storm could come any night. What should Bryn change before the skippers trust the predictor again? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add Tuesday's storm to the 13 and retrain at degree 12, so the predictor never misses a storm like that again.
options.part2: I added Tuesday's storm and retrained at degree 12. Fourteen storms and 13 numbers to tune, so the replay was no longer perfect, but every storm came back within 5 knots, and Tuesday's within one. I felt better for five days. On Sunday evening the barometer fell 2.0 hPa, the kind of fall that brought 13 to 17 knots in our log. The predictor said 47. Every boat stayed in for a light blow, and on Monday the skippers stopped asking me.
options.senior: Adding the miss to the training data teaches the model that one storm, not the pattern. A curve with almost as many numbers as storms still memorizes, so it just goes wild in the next gap. Fix how you train and test, not the last mistake.

options.text: Type in the paper logbooks. Hold storms back, try every degree, and keep the one that misses the held-back storms least. Lock a last pile away for one final check.
options.part2: I typed in all 65 paper storms, 79 with the logbook and Tuesday's. I held back one pile for choosing the degree and locked a smaller one in the desk drawer. On the choosing pile, the typical miss was lowest at a gently bent curve, nothing like 12, and the drawer pile agreed when I opened it once, at the end. It misses most storms by 3 or 4 knots now, the ones it trained on included, and I trust it more than the one that was never wrong. Back on Wednesday, on the six storms I'd held back, degree 12 had missed by 39.9 knots and degree 3 by 3.4, and degree 3 would have called Tuesday 51. Last night, out of curiosity, I asked the old degree-12 file about a fall of 1.8 hPa, an ordinary windy evening. It said minus 139 knots. I haven't deleted it. I can't say why.
options.senior: Training error measures memory; only error on examples the model never saw measures skill. Choose the model on one held-back pile, confirm it once on another, and prefer the simplest model that does well. More examples make memorizing harder for every model.

options.text: Set the degree to 1. A straight line can't memorize anything, so it can never forecast an impossible wind.
options.part2: I set it to a straight line. It never said anything strange again. It also never got the shape: it called the quiet nights too windy and the middle storms too calm. For Tuesday it would have said 44 knots, 14 short, and on the six storms I'd held back it missed by about 8 knots, typically, where a gently curved line missed by about 3. The skippers started adding ten knots on the big nights.
options.senior: A model too simple for the pattern underfits: steady, but wrong the same way every time. The goal isn't the simplest possible model. It's the one that does best on examples it has never seen.

options.text: The logger also recorded humidity, sea temperature and wind direction on those nights. Give the predictor all of them as features, so it has more to learn from.
options.part2: I gave the predictor everything the logger had: four features for each of the 13 storms. With more to work with, it reached a perfect replay at a lower degree. On Friday the glass fell almost exactly as fast as in 2021, when we had 44 knots. The predictor forecast a calm night, because the sea that evening was a degree warmer than on any storm it had seen. We got 41.
options.senior: More features with the same handful of examples give a model more ways to memorize coincidences. Features pay off when there are enough examples to tell a real pattern from luck. With 13 storms, almost anything matches something.

sim.title: Fit the storms yourself
sim.lede: You're Bryn on Wednesday night. Each dot is one storm: how far the barometer fell in the 3 hours before (across) and the strongest gust that followed (up). Light dots are the 13 logbook storms, the training set. Red dots are the test set, held back: Tuesday's storm, ringed, and the five you typed in from the paper logbooks. The solid line is the model's curve at the degree you pick, and the dashed red line is its miss on Tuesday. Errors are typical misses in knots, the way u/gradient_ghost described: the typical miss on the training set is the training error, and on the test set the test error. The lower chart shows both at every degree at once. Storms you type in later are a teaching model: drawn from the hidden pattern plus random noise, not copied from real pages.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start at degree 12, Tuesday's setting: training error 0.0, test error 39.9, and a forecast of -13 knots for Tuesday. Slide down to 1: a straight line, too simple to follow the shape (engineers call that underfitting), so it's wrong on both piles. Find the degree with the lowest test error (the green ring on the lower chart) and read Tuesday's forecast there. Choosing the degree by these six storms turns them into a validation set: the winner's 3.4 is a little flattered, which is why the senior answer locks a last pile away. Then go back to 12 and type in 10 storms three times: with 34 storms to train on, 13 numbers can't memorize them all, and the gap closes. Reshuffle to hold back different storms and watch the lowest point move. Last, show the hidden pattern.

explain.oneLine: Nothing haunted the predictor. Given 13 numbers to tune for 13 storms, it bent its curve through every one of them, noise and all, so it was perfect on the past and lost in the gap where Tuesday's storm fell.

steps.title: AI, machine learning and deep learning are boxes inside boxes.
steps.text: Artificial intelligence, AI, is the broad goal: programs that solve tasks we'd call intelligent. Some AI is rules a person wrote into a program, like a warning that fires whenever the barometer falls fast. Machine learning is one way to build AI, and the one behind most AI today: instead of writing the rule, you train a model on examples and let it find the rule. Google's own course uses weather as its example. Rather than computing the physics of the whole atmosphere, you give a model lots of weather data until it learns the relationship. Deep learning is one kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers, and the next case opens one up. Bryn's curve is machine learning, but not deep learning.

steps.title: Data, features and labels: what Bryn gave it.
steps.text: Bryn's data was 13 examples, one per storm. Each example has a feature, the input the model sees (how far the barometer fell in three hours), and a label, the answer it should learn to give (the strongest gust that followed). Real models usually have many features: Google's course describes a rainfall model whose features could include temperature, humidity, wind direction and air pressure, with the rainfall amount as the label. Nobody wrote the rule from feature to label. The model is that rule, learned from examples: a function, not a list of instructions.

steps.title: Training comes first. Inference happens every night after.
steps.text: Training fits the model to labeled examples. Bryn's program used least squares: of all the curves of the chosen degree, it picks the one whose squared misses on the training storms add up to the least. A degree-12 curve has 13 numbers to tune, its parameters. Then the model is frozen. Inference is using it: you hand it only a feature, Tuesday's 7.5 hPa, and it hands back a prediction, minus 13 knots. It learns nothing while it answers. A model only changes when someone trains it again.

steps.title: Thirteen numbers for thirteen storms: overfitting.
steps.text: Every storm is the hidden pattern plus noise. With as many numbers to tune as there are storms, least squares can pass the curve exactly through all 13, so it does: it memorizes the noise along with the pattern. Between storms, nothing holds it in place. In the empty stretch from 6.5 to 9.0 hPa it dives from 44 knots to minus 13 at Tuesday's 7.5 and about minus 18 just past it. At 1.8 hPa, a windy evening, it says minus 139. On the six storms it never saw, Tuesday's and five from the paper logbooks, its typical miss is 39.9 knots, against 0.0 on the 13 it studied. Go the other way, to degree 1, and you get underfitting: a straight line misses the training storms by 5.7 knots and the new ones by 7.8, because it can't draw the pattern's S-shape. Degree 3 misses them by 3.6 and 3.4.

steps.title: Generalization is the only score that counts.
steps.text: Generalization is how well a model does on data it never trained on, and you can only measure it with examples held back from training. Training error never rises as you add bends, because each bend is one more way to chase the storms you already have. Test error falls while the curve is learning the real shape, then climbs once it starts learning noise: the lower chart in the sim. Two things push the lowest point your way. More data helps, because 34 storms can't all be memorized by 13 numbers. Simpler models help, because they can't memorize much at all. Large language models learn the same way at a vast scale: their examples are text, the feature is the words so far, and the label is the next word (strictly, the next token, a small piece of text). Case 6 of this season goes deep.

diagram.aria: Training versus testing and inference. Training comes first: the 13 logbook storms, each with a feature (the fall) and a label (the gust), go into training by least squares, which tunes 13 numbers. Replaying the same storms gives a training error of 0.0 knots, a measure of memory. Training produces the model, a degree-12 curve, frozen after training. The 6 held-back storms, Tuesday's and 5 from the paper logbooks, are scored by the model for a test error of 39.9 knots. Asked about Tuesday at 01:40, a fall of 7.5 hPa with no label, the model answers minus 13 knots; the gauge measured 58.

explain.caption: Read top to bottom. Training comes first: least squares tunes the curve's 13 numbers to the 13 logbook storms, and replaying those same storms gives a training error of 0.0 knots, which only measures memory. Then the model is frozen. Testing grades it on six storms it never saw: a typical miss of 39.9 knots. Inference is asking it about a new storm: minus 13 knots for Tuesday, when 58 came.

fix.title: The fix: never grade a model on what it studied
fix.text: Split the storms before training. Train on one pile, the training set. Choose the degree, and any other setting, by the typical miss on a second pile it never trains on, which engineers call a validation set. Keep a third pile, the test set, locked away and use it once, at the end, to say how good the predictor really is. Among the settings that do well on held-back storms, pick the simplest, because a curve with fewer numbers to tune can't memorize noise. Another standard tool, regularization, penalizes complexity during training for the same reason. Then get more examples: with 79 storms instead of 13, even a bendy curve can't pass through every one, so it has to find the shape they share. Keep checking after launch, storm by storm, because the past only predicts the future while the weather behaves like the past.

limits: A held-back score only predicts the future if new examples look like the old ones. Google's course lists the conditions: examples that don't influence each other, data that doesn't change much over time, and training, test and real-world data that are statistically similar. A new wind gauge, a moved hut or a changing climate breaks them, and the test score quietly stops meaning anything.

A test set wears out. Every decision made by looking at it fits the model a little more closely to those particular storms, so the more often you reuse it, the less it tells you. That's why the last pile stays locked away.

With six held-back storms the score itself is noisy: one odd storm can flatter or sink a model, which is why reshuffling the split in the sim moves the lowest point around. More data, and averaging over several different splits, steady it.

head: What matters
Simple model (degree 1 to 3)
Complex model (degree 10 to 12)
rows: On the storms it trained on
Misses by a few knots. It can't follow every bump.
Misses by almost nothing. At degree 12 with 13 storms, by exactly nothing.
About as good as on its training storms, as long as it isn't too simple.
Can be wildly wrong, worst in the gaps between examples: minus 13 knots for Tuesday.
Underfits when the real pattern has more shape than it can draw: degree 1 missed the six new storms by about 8 knots.
Overfits: it learns the noise along with the pattern.
Works with a handful of examples.
For curves like Bryn's, many more examples than numbers to tune. Big neural networks bend this rule (case 8), but held-back error stays the judge.
Swings hard, because nothing in its examples holds it in place.

explain.seniorTake: Training error is a measure of memory, not skill. The only number that predicts tomorrow is error on examples the model never saw, measured on data that looks like tomorrow, and spent sparingly. Start simple, add complexity only while held-back error keeps falling, and when a model is perfect on its training data, treat that as a question, not an answer.

realWorld.title: Google Flu Trends, the winter detector
realWorld.text: Google Flu Trends estimated flu activity from what people searched for, and was built to predict the reports of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on doctor visits for influenza-like illness. In a 2014 paper in *Science*, Lazer, Kennedy, King and Vespignani described what went wrong. The first version came from finding the best matches among 50 million search terms to fit 1,152 data points, and its developers had to weed out terms that rose and fell with the flu season but had nothing to do with flu, such as searches about high school basketball. The authors call that a warning that the big data were overfitting the small number of cases, and say the first version was part flu detector, part winter detector. It completely missed the 2009 A-H1N1 pandemic, which didn't follow the usual season. An updated version ran from 2009. In February 2013, *Nature* reported it was predicting more than double the share of doctor visits that the CDC reported, and from 21 August 2011 to 1 September 2013 it estimated too high in 100 of 108 weeks. The authors blame that later drift mostly on changes Google made to its own search engine, not on overfitting: the searches stopped looking like the ones the model was built on. A model built from the CDC's own earlier reports and the time of year did better: over a held-back period, its mean absolute error was 0.311 against 0.486 for Google Flu Trends, and combining the two gave 0.232.

realWorld.title: Google's Machine Learning Crash Course
realWorld.text: Google's course defines overfitting as creating a model that matches, or memorizes, the training set so closely that it fails to make correct predictions on new data, and generalization as the opposite: a model that generalizes well makes good predictions on new data. It shows a cousin of the sim's lower chart: loss curves, which plot error as training goes on rather than by degree. For the training set and a held-back validation set they behave alike at first, then the training loss keeps falling or holds steady while the validation loss rises. It names two broad causes, a training set that doesn't represent real-life data and a model that is too complex, and its page on model complexity says simple models typically do better than complex ones on the test set.

realWorld.title: Language models are trained the same way
realWorld.text: OpenAI's 2019 GPT-2 paper describes language modeling as estimating the probability of a piece of text one symbol at a time, each symbol given the ones before it. Its examples were WebText, a dataset of millions of webpages, and its largest model had 1.5 billion parameters, against the 13 that Bryn's curve tuned. The recipe is the one in this case: examples, a model with parameters, training, then inference on text it has never seen. Even so, the paper reports that the 1.5-billion-parameter model still underfits WebText's 40 GB of text.

asked: Your RAG system's eval scores look great, but users say the answers in production are bad. What's happening?
What are overfitting and underfitting, and how do you detect and fix each?
interview.answer: Treat it as a generalization problem. The eval set probably doesn't look like production: it was written by the team, drawn from the same documents and question styles used while building, or reused so often that prompts and settings were tuned to it, which is overfitting to the eval. Ask where the eval questions came from, when they were written, and how many decisions were made by looking at them. Then sample real production questions, label a fresh held-out set from them, and compare. A big gap between the eval score and the fresh score is the same gap as a curve that's perfect on 13 storms. Fix it by refreshing the eval from real traffic, keeping a locked set that nobody tunes against, and watching quality in production. For the classic question: underfitting is high error on both the training data and held-out data, so add complexity or better features; overfitting is low training error with much higher held-out error, so simplify, regularize or add data. Choose by held-out error, never by training error. LATENT's Season 5 goes deep on evals.

terms.def: The broad goal of programs that solve tasks we'd call intelligent, like translating text or forecasting a storm. Some AI follows rules a person wrote. Most of today's AI is machine learning.
Short for artificial intelligence.
A way of building AI where a program learns its rule from examples instead of being given one. Google calls it training software, a model, to make useful predictions from data.
One kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. It powers today's language and image models. The next case opens one up.
A model built from many small connected units arranged in layers, each passing numbers to the next. Case 2 of this season shows how one learns.
What training produces: a learned function that turns features into a prediction. Bryn's model is a curve, and nobody wrote its rule by hand.
A rule that turns an input into an output. A trained model is a function learned from examples.
Recorded facts a model learns from, such as the station's logbook.
A collection of examples kept together for training or testing a model.
One item of data: here, one storm with its feature (how far the barometer fell) and its label (the strongest gust that followed).
An input the model uses to make its prediction. Bryn's predictor has one: how far the barometer fell in the 3 hours before.
The answer the model should learn to give for an example. Here, the strongest gust in the 12 hours after the fall.
Adjusting a model's parameters so its predictions match the labels of its training examples. It happens before the model is used.
Using a trained model on new input to get a prediction, like asking Bryn's predictor about Tuesday's 7.5 hPa. The model learns nothing while it answers.
A model's output for one input: its best guess at the label. Called a forecast when it's about the future.
Bryn's name for the station's model: the program that turns a barometer fall into a forecast gust.
A number inside a model that training tunes. Bryn's degree-12 curve has 13. Large language models have billions.
The line a model like Bryn's draws through the storms. Reading the curve's height at a barometer fall gives the forecast gust.
For a curve like Bryn's, how bendy it may be. Degree 1 is a straight line. Degree 12 can bend 11 times and has 13 numbers to tune.
How flexible a model is: how many shapes it can draw. More complexity fits training data better but makes memorizing noise easier.
The standard way to fit a curve: of all the curves allowed, choose the one whose squared misses on the training examples add up to the least.
The examples a model is trained on.
Examples held back from training and used to measure how well the model does on data it has never seen. It only works if nobody tunes against it.
A second held-back pile used to choose settings like the degree, so the test set stays untouched for the final check.
Kept out of training on purpose, so the examples can measure the model fairly. Also called held out.
Dividing the examples into piles, such as a training set and a test set, before training starts.
When a model fits its training examples so closely, noise and all, that it does badly on new data: low training error, much higher test error.
When a model is too simple to follow the real pattern, so it misses both its training examples and new ones.
How well a model does on new data it never trained on. The opposite of overfitting, and the only score that predicts real use.
The relationship every example shares, like bigger pressure falls bringing stronger gusts. A good model learns the pattern, not the noise.
In the sim, the true shape the storms come from. Real data never shows it to you; you only see examples scattered around it.
The part of each example the pattern can't explain: a gust off the cliff, a sticky needle, luck. A model that learns the noise has memorized.
For a model, to fit each training example exactly, noise included, instead of learning the pattern they share.
How far a model's predictions are from the true labels, summed up in some way. Lower is better.
This case's plain name for root mean square error: square each miss, average them, take the square root. Big misses count extra.
The typical miss on the examples the model trained on. It measures memory more than skill.
The typical miss on held-back examples the model never trained on: the honest estimate of how it will do on new data.
Test error minus training error. A big gap is the signature of overfitting.
A training technique that penalizes a model for being complex, nudging it toward simpler fits to prevent overfitting.
A single number saying how wrong a model's predictions are on some examples. Training tries to make it small. Case 2 of this season looks closer.
A chart of loss as training goes on, drawn separately for the training set and a held-back set. When the two curves part, the model is overfitting.
A simplified setup that shows the shape of real behavior, not real measurements. The storms you type in during the sim are one.
A model that estimates how likely a piece of text is, one piece at a time, each given the ones before. It is trained on huge amounts of text.
A very large language model, with billions of parameters, like the ones behind chat assistants. Also called an LLM. This course is about building with them.
A small piece of text, often a word or part of a word, that a language model reads and predicts. Case 3 of this season covers tokens.
How likely something is, as a number from 0 (it never happens) to 1 (it always happens).
The text you send a language model to ask it something or tell it what to do.
A 2019 language model from OpenAI. Its paper describes training on WebText, a dataset of millions of webpages; its largest version had 1.5 billion parameters.
An AI company. It published the GPT-2 paper in 2019.
Retrieval-augmented generation: an AI system that looks up relevant documents and hands them to a language model along with the question. Season 3 builds one.
A test of an AI system's quality: usually a set of questions with known good answers and a way to score the system's responses. Season 5 is about evals.
The live system that real users rely on, as opposed to development or testing.
The value at which a monitoring system raises an alarm, like a server being more than 90% busy. Tuning it only on last month's graphs can overfit last month.
How much water vapour the air holds.
An instrument that measures air pressure. A fast fall in pressure often means a storm is coming.
Sailors' old word for the barometer. "The glass is falling" means the pressure is dropping.
The weight of the air above you, measured by a barometer. Storms come with low pressure.
Hectopascal, the usual unit of air pressure in weather reports. A fall of several hPa in 3 hours is fast.
A speed of one nautical mile an hour, about 1.85 km an hour. Wind at sea is measured in knots.
A short burst of wind stronger than the wind around it. The strongest gust is what breaks things.
An instrument that measures wind speed, often with spinning cups on a mast. Also called an anemometer.
A small device that records an instrument's readings automatically, so nobody has to write them down.
The station's record of readings. Before the logger, observers wrote them by hand.
The person in charge of a boat.
A stone landing where boats tie up.
A Google service that estimated flu activity from what people searched for. A 2014 paper in Science analyzed why it overestimated.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the US public health agency whose doctor-visit reports Google Flu Trends was built to predict.
A fever with a cough or sore throat. The CDC tracks the share of doctor visits for it to follow the flu season. Often shortened to ILI.
The words someone types into a search engine.
Very large datasets, often collected for another purpose, like search logs. The Flu Trends paper warns that size doesn't replace careful measurement.
A disease outbreak that spreads across many countries. The 2009 A-H1N1 flu pandemic didn't follow the usual flu season.
The average size of a model's misses, ignoring whether they were too high or too low. Lower is better.
A leading peer-reviewed scientific journal. The Google Flu Trends analysis appeared in it in March 2014.
A leading peer-reviewed scientific journal. In February 2013 it reported Google Flu Trends' large overestimate.
Google's free online course on machine learning, used in this case as a reference for overfitting, generalization and splitting data.

atWork: Find one rule at work that was tuned by looking at the past: an alert threshold nudged until it fired on every bad night last month, a cut-off score for spam or fraud, or an actual machine learning model. Write down what data it was tuned on, and whether anyone ever checked it on a period it never saw. Then do that check: replay a different month, a later one if you can, and count how often it fires wrongly or stays silent, compared with the month it was tuned on. If your team runs a model, find where its training and test data come from, confirm no example appears in both, and confirm the test examples come from after the training ones. A big gap between the two scores is overfitting, at work.

recall.prompt: A teammate built a model that predicts how many minutes late each delivery will be. On the 2,000 past deliveries it trained on, its typical miss is 0.4 minutes. They want to ship it on Monday. What do you ask, and what do you check first?

keyIdeas.idea: That number is training error: it measures memory, not skill
Score it on held-back deliveries it never trained on, ideally the most recent ones
A big gap between training and test error means overfitting: simplify, regularize or get more data
Check that the test data looks like what it will face on Monday

recall.model: 0.4 minutes on the deliveries it trained on is training error: it tells me how well it remembers, not how well it predicts. Before Monday I'd hold back deliveries it never trained on, ideally the most recent few weeks so the test looks like what it will face, and measure the typical miss there. If that's far above 0.4, it's overfitting: I'd try a simpler model, regularization or more data, and choose the setting with the lowest error on held-back data. Then I'd confirm it once on a final set nobody tuned against. Only that last number says what Monday will look like.

recall.prompt: On the 13 storms it trained on, Bryn's degree-12 curve had a typical miss of 0.0 knots. On six storms it had never seen, 39.9. What is that?
options: Underfitting: the curve was too simple
Generalization: it learned the pattern well
Overfitting: it memorized the 13 storms, noise and all
Inference: the model was still training
recall.why: A model that fits its training examples perfectly but misses new ones badly has memorized them instead of learning the pattern. The 39.9-knot gap between the two scores is the signature of overfitting.

recall.prompt: A bakery wants a model that predicts tomorrow's loaves sold from the weather forecast and the day of the week. It has two years of daily sales. Name the features and the label, say what training and inference are here, and how you'd check the model before trusting it.

keyIdeas.idea: Features: the weather forecast and the day of the week
Label: the number of loaves sold
Training fits it to past days with known sales; inference predicts tomorrow
Check it on held-back days it never trained on

recall.model: The features are tomorrow's weather forecast, such as temperature and rain, and the day of the week. The label is the number of loaves sold that day. Training fits the model to two years of past days, each with its features and the loaves actually sold. Inference is each evening: feed it tomorrow's forecast and weekday and read off the prediction. Before trusting it, I'd hold back the most recent few months as a test set, train on the rest, and compare its typical miss on those months with its miss on the training days. If the test miss is much bigger, it's overfitting.

options: Tuning the curve's 13 numbers to the logbook storms
Asking the finished predictor what Tuesday's 7.5 hPa fall will bring
Typing the paper logbooks into the computer
Choosing which storms to hold back
recall.why: Inference is using a trained model on a new input to get a prediction. Tuning the numbers is training, typing in logbooks is gathering data, and choosing which storms to hold back is splitting it.

recall.prompt: How do AI, machine learning and deep learning fit together?
options: They are three names for the same thing
Deep learning contains machine learning, which contains AI
Machine learning and deep learning are separate fields that both replaced AI
Deep learning is one kind of machine learning, and machine learning is one way of building AI
recall.why: They nest. AI is the broad goal, machine learning builds it by learning from examples, and deep learning is machine learning with many-layered neural networks. Some AI, like rules a person wrote, isn't machine learning at all.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The predictor now learns from 79 storms, with 20 held back as a test set. All winter Ludo, a student who volunteers at the station, worked on it: each evening he changed one thing (the degree, which old storms to include, an extra feature), checked the typical miss on the same 20 held-back storms, and kept whatever made it smaller. Forty tries later it was down from 3.6 knots to 2.1, and he called it the best predictor on the coast. On the first three storms of spring it missed by 7, 9 and 6 knots.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What happened to Ludo's 2.1, and how should he have run the winter?

keyIdeas.idea: Choosing by the same 20 storms forty times fitted the model to them: they weren't unseen anymore
Choose settings on one held-back pile and keep a final test set locked away, used once
Spring storms may not look like the ones he tuned on

coldCase.model: His 2.1 stopped being a fair score after the first few tries. Every time he kept a change because it helped on the same 20 storms, a little of those 20 leaked into his choices, so after forty tries he had tuned the predictor to them: the same overfitting, one level up. The spring misses of 6 to 9 knots are closer to the truth. He should have split three ways: train on one pile, choose settings by the typical miss on a second pile, and keep a third pile locked away and use it once, at the end, to say how good the predictor really is. And that final pile should include storms like the ones coming, because spring storms may not look like the winter ones he tuned on.
